part_title: Lambda Workload Choices, Five Patterns, Runtimes, Triggers and OpenSearch

scenes.title: When Lambda fits your workload
scenes.narration: The question on this slide is simple: when is Lambda the right compute choice? Look at the three columns. On the left, we have sporadic file uploads. A file arrives in storage, Lambda processes it, and the result is saved or indexed. The function only needs to run when work exists, so this is a natural event-driven pattern. In the middle, the workload is very different: a predictable process runs continuously for a long time. Keeping a container or server running may be more suitable than repeatedly starting short-lived functions. On the right, we have a bursty API. Some minutes are quiet, and suddenly many users make requests. Lambda can scale concurrent executions to handle that changing demand, within its limits. The decision diagram across the bottom summarises these trade-offs. For occasional, short tasks, prefer Lambda. For sustained, long-running processing, consider a container or server. For variable API traffic, Lambda can be a strong option. One detail the visual doesn't show is that scaling the function doesn't automatically scale a database or Bedrock model behind it. Always consider the limits of the whole application. The takeaway is not that serverless is always best; it's that the right compute choice follows the workload.

scenes.title: Five useful Lambda patterns
scenes.narration: This slide gives us five practical ways to use Lambda. Read the columns from left to right and compare the input with the output. First is S3 object-event processing. When a new image arrives in a bucket, Lambda can resize it and save a thumbnail. Second is stream enrichment. A DynamoDB change record is received, enriched with additional information, and written to another data store. Third is data transformation. A raw CSV file becomes structured JSON ready for the next processing step. Fourth is a scheduled task. EventBridge can trigger a function at a configured time, perhaps generating a daily report and placing it in S3. The fifth pattern is reacting to an AWS service event, such as an EC2 state change. A function could update a record, alert a team, or start a follow-up workflow. The useful comparison is that Lambda performs small units of business logic, but the event sources are different. Look at the takeaway along the bottom: choose the trigger first, then make your handler idempotent. Why? An event can be retried or delivered more than once, and a second execution should not cause an unwanted duplicate action.

scenes.title: Choose a Lambda runtime
scenes.narration: Now let's look at how we actually write the function. The slide compares Python on the left with Node.js in the middle. Both examples receive an event and context, read a name from the event, and return a result containing a greeting and the original input. Notice that the syntax differs, but the job is identical: accept an event, execute handler code, and return a response. The panel on the right introduces a custom runtime or container image for cases where the standard runtime doesn't provide the language, system libraries, or environment you need. That choice brings more responsibility for packaging and maintaining dependencies. Across the bottom, follow the development sequence: select the runtime, write the handler, create a test event, and inspect CloudWatch logs. This is a useful debugging habit. If the function isn't producing the expected JSON, check what event it actually received and what the handler logged. Also remember that runtime choice does not grant AWS permissions. A Python or Node.js function that calls S3 or Bedrock still needs an execution role allowing those operations. The core idea: choose the environment that supports your code, then test the full event-to-result path.

scenes.title: Understand Lambda triggers
scenes.narration: This slide compares two very different ways a Lambda function receives work. On the left is push invocation. Services such as API Gateway, S3 event notifications or EventBridge send an event that invokes the function. Trace the arrows: the service emits an event, and Lambda runs the handler. On the right is a poll-based event source mapping. Lambda polls a service such as SQS or Kinesis for records, collects messages or a batch, and invokes your function with those records. The distinction matters when something fails. For a synchronous API request, the caller may be waiting for a response. For SQS, an unsuccessful batch can become available again after the visibility timeout. With a Kinesis stream, failed record processing can affect progress through the shard. The lower part of the slide calls out retries and failure destinations. Don't assume an event is delivered exactly once. Build idempotent handlers, inspect which records succeeded, and configure an appropriate dead-letter queue or failure handling where that integration supports it. So before writing Lambda code, ask who sends or polls the event. That tells you a great deal about batching, retries, and the user's experience.

scenes.title: Lambda and OpenSearch indexing
scenes.narration: Here we connect Lambda to a retrieval system for generative AI. Follow the top pipeline from left to right. Documents such as FAQs, policies and manuals are uploaded to S3. Lambda acts as ingestion glue: it reads a document, extracts its content, and splits the text into manageable chunks. An embedding model converts those chunks into numeric vectors representing their meaning. OpenSearch stores the vectors together with the source text and metadata, and later returns relevant content when the application searches. Now look at the detailed example along the bottom. The source document describes a return policy, including a thirty-day return window and a requirement for proof of purchase. The next panel breaks that policy into individual chunks. Beside it are small arrays of embedding numbers and an example index record with a chunk identifier, text, embedding and source metadata. Finally, the retrieval panel shows a matching policy passage returned to the application. An AI model can use that retrieved passage as evidence when answering a customer's question. Lambda isn't the search engine and doesn't generate the embedding by itself; it coordinates the steps and can retry failed ingestion safely. Stable document and chunk identifiers help prevent duplicate index records.
